power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: A recent paper (Minkov, 2026) claimed that great ape personality is not well-described by the five personality dimensions found in humans, those being Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness to Experience, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness.
text.formatted: A recent paper <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Minkov, 2026)</ref> claimed that great ape personality is not well-described by the five personality dimensions found in humans, those being Neuroticism, Extraversion, Openness to Experience, Agreeableness, and Conscientiousness.

text.text: To support this claim, the author analyzed personality factor structures obtained in studies of great apes in which personality was assessed using rating scales.

The analyses tested for 'configural invariance' by computing the percentage of traits that loaded on the same factor as in humans in chimpanzees, orangutans, mountain gorillas, and bonobos, and the percentage of traits that loaded on the same factor across four studies of chimpanzees.

The paper also reviewed the evidence for Conscientiousness in chimpanzees, including by citing the results of studies that used other ratings scales, and concluded that this factor's evidentiary basis was weak.
The paper concluded by proposing an alternative approach to studying personality in great apes.
This commentary exposes fundamental problems with the article.
First, I show that the paper's author mischaracterized the research program of comparative psychologists who study personality.
Second, I review the evidence the paper uses to support its claim that there is little evidence for configural invariance, highlighting problems and errors in the analyses and reporting of results.
Third, I review the evidence presented against the presence of Conscientiousness in chimpanzees and find it problematic.
Finally, I demonstrate that the literature review lacks due care.
I conclude by dispelling a misunderstanding about comparative research on personality and reaffirm the importance and promise of scientific pluralism.
Michael Minkov (M.M.), in his article, criticized the work of some comparative psychologists who study great ape personality (Minkov, 2026).
text.formatted: Michael Minkov (M.M.), in his article, criticized the work of some comparative psychologists who study great ape personality <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Minkov, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: To do so, he, as stated in abbreviated form in a summary point, claimed that "Many studies suggest that the human Five Factor/Big Five personality model has partial or near-complete analogs in great ape personality." (Minkov, 2026, p. 2).
text.formatted: To do so, he, as stated in abbreviated form in a summary point, claimed that "Many studies suggest that the human Five Factor/Big Five personality model has partial or near-complete analogs in great ape personality." <ref type="bibr">(Minkov, 2026, p. 2)</ref>.

text.text: Next, based on his analyses and a review of the literature, M.M. concluded that the Five-Factor Model, a personality structure found in humans (McCrae & Costa, 2008) is "not appropriate for describing great ape personality." (Minkov, 2026, p. 16).
text.formatted: Next, based on his analyses and a review of the literature, M.M. concluded that the Five-Factor Model, a personality structure found in humans <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(McCrae & Costa, 2008)</ref> is "not appropriate for describing great ape personality." <ref type="bibr">(Minkov, 2026, p. 16)</ref>.

text.text: In this commentary I first show that the claims in M.M.'s paper (the critique) with regards to what these comparative psychologists claim amounts to a strawman (strawape?).
Next, I show how problems with M.M.'s analyses in his critique lead to vastly different conclusions than the literature supports.
Finally, I highlight other problems with M.M.'s critique before setting the record straight.
In his critique, M.M. mischaracterized how comparative psychologists who study great apes interpreted results from their studies.

For instance, King and Figueredo (1997) obtained personality ratings in 100 zoo-housed chimpanzees using a broad instrument measure derived by sampling and adapting traits from Goldberg's (1990) trait taxonomy.
text.formatted: For instance, <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">King and Figueredo (1997)</ref> obtained personality ratings in 100 zoo-housed chimpanzees using a broad instrument measure derived by sampling and adapting traits from <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Goldberg's (1990)</ref> trait taxonomy.

text.text: Their exploratory factor analysis identified six personality factors, with five bearing some resemblance to the Five-Factor Model domains (see Table 1 in King & Figueredo, 1997).
text.formatted: Their exploratory factor analysis identified six personality factors, with five bearing some resemblance to the Five-Factor Model domains (see Table <ref type="table">1</ref> in <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">King & Figueredo, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: On page 1 of the critique, M.M. stated that King and Figueredo "concluded that their results 'supported an interpretation of these factors consistent with the human Big Five' (p. 266)."
The cited quote, however, was taken out of context.
On page 266 of their article, it is clear that King and Figueredo (1997 offered a highly nuanced view of what similarities, where they exist, might and might not mean
The descriptors placed in the chimpanzee factors two through six supported an interpretation of these factors consistent with the human Big Five.
However, as noted before, nine items had their highest loadings on factors different from those in the Goldberg (1990) taxonomy.
text.formatted: However, as noted before, nine items had their highest loadings on factors different from those in the <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Goldberg (1990)</ref> taxonomy.

text.text: The deviations from the human pattern of factor loadings may be partly attributable to differences between the meanings of some descriptors depending upon whether they are applied to humans or to chimpanzees.

For example, the adjective "lazy" when applied to humans has connotations of irresponsibility and a preference of play over work, failings that are consistent with its placement at the negative pole of the human dependability factor.
However, these two human attributes cannot be meaningfully applied to chimpanzees.

Consequently, the raters' attributions of laziness to chimpanzees probably involved a narrowed definition centered around perceived lethargy and lack of activity, characteristics consistent with the negative pole of the surgency factor.
Similarly nuanced interpretations have been voiced in reviews of the primate personality literature (Freeman & Gosling, 2010; Weiss, 2018).
text.formatted: Similarly nuanced interpretations have been voiced in reviews of the primate personality literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Freeman & Gosling, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Weiss, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Like King and Figueredo, the authors of these reviews explicitly pointed out that, although there are varying degrees of overlap, great ape species and other primates have personality structures that differ from humans, and from one another.
These observations led to systematic studies of personality differences across related taxa (Adams et al., 2015; Masilkova et al., 2020; Weiss et al., 2026).
text.formatted: These observations led to systematic studies of personality differences across related taxa <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Masilkova et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Weiss et al., 2026</ref>).

text.text: To take another example, M.M. mischaracterized the point of my paper "A human model for primate personality" (Weiss, 2017b).
text.formatted: To take another example, M.M. mischaracterized the point of my paper "A human model for primate personality" <ref type="bibr">(Weiss, 2017b)</ref>.

text.text: M.M. cited this paper as suggesting that the human Five-Factor Model is applicable to great apes.
M.M. and backed this assertion with another quote taken out of context, i.e., "the human model has been successful when applied to the study of primates" (Weiss 2017, 6)" (Minkov, 2026, p. 2).
text.formatted: M.M. and backed this assertion with another quote taken out of context, i.e., "the human model has been successful when applied to the study of primates" <ref type="bibr">(Weiss 2017, 6</ref>)" <ref type="bibr">(Minkov, 2026, p. 2)</ref>.

text.text: Here, the deviation is extreme.
The "human model" referred to is not the Five-Factor Model or Big Five as M.M.'s critique would have one believe.

Instead, it refers to the more general idea, developed in studies of humans, that correlated questionnaire items, behaviors, and other purported measures of personality are manifestations of a smaller number of factors, and that critical questions should focus on "what underlying dimensions these measures identify, how much genetic and environmental influences contribute to these differences, and the behavioural, real-world and fitness consequences of these differences" (Weiss, 2017b, p. 2).

text.text: This is why, to understand what the factors of a given species are, researchers study relationships between personality factors and outcomes following the same logic, and often reaching similar conclusions, of a study of depression (Xu et al., 2015) that M.M., paradoxically, cites favorably (Minkov, 2026, p. 3).

text.text: For example, correlations between personality factors and subjective well-being in orangutans found that three of the five factors were correlated with subjective well-being in a manner consistent with what one would expect: higher Extraversion and Agreeableness and lower Neuroticism were associated with higher subjective well-being (Weiss et al., 2006).

text.text: Moving on, M.M.'s critique reported results from tests of configural invariance-whether the same items load on the same factors in two or more samples.
The author operationalized these tests by calculating the percent of items in two samples that shared a primary-factor loading (the size and direction of a between an item and a factor).

M.M.'s first set of tests compared factor assignments of the items in humans against loadings from studies of zoo-housed chimpanzees, orangutans, and bonobos, and from a study of wild mountain gorillas.

M.M.'s second set of these tests compared item assignments in humans to factor loadings from four independent studies of chimpanzees, and compared the loadings from the chimpanzee studies to one another.
The results of these tests seemed to show that the percentage of items on matching factors tends to be low (see Tables 2 and 4 in Minkov, 2026).

text.text: M.M. interpreted these findings as evidence of structural differences between human and great ape personality, and between the personality structures obtained in independent samples of chimpanzees.
Close examination of these tests, however, reveals that they are invalid.

The primary defect of M.M.'s analyses relates to the assumption that previous studies of personality in great apes (e.g., King & Figueredo, 1997) attempted to find the Five-Factor Model or claimed that the factors found in great apes were identical to it.

text.text: The second defect is that the assignment of items to human factors is incorrect at times.
To see how this flaw produces incorrect conclusions, consider the item cool 1 .
In Table 2 of M.M.'s critique, cool is designated as a marker of low Extraversion.

text.text: The fact that it does not load on Extraversion in great ape samples is therefore taken as evidence of misfit.

However, although cool refers to aloofness or a lack of interpersonal warmth in many human personality taxonomies (see, e.g., Table 1 in Goldberg, 1990), the item cool, which was introduced in the Orangutan Personality Questionnaire (OPQ; Weiss et al., 2006, p. 504) and included in the Hominoid Personality Questionnaire (HPQ; Weiss, 2017a; Weiss et al., 2009), was designed to measure low Neuroticism.

text.text: A third defect is that of selective reporting.
One illustration of this problem concerns the item bullying.

M.M.'s critique, in Table 4, reported no overlap for this item across four chimpanzee studies: the item is related to Dominance in one study (King & Figueredo, 1997), not included in two studies (Dutton, 2008; Weiss et al., 2017), and related to Neuroticism in a fourth study (Freeman et al., 2013).

text.text: The fourth problem is an assumption inherent in the author's use of percentages to examine invariance, i.e., that each and every trait is related to just one factor.

text.text: There are better methods to compare the personality structures of different samples.
One is to use targeted orthogonal Procrustes rotation (Schönemann, 1966) as have McCrae et al. (1996).

text.text: This method does not assume simple structure and works by finding orthogonal axes-to avoid overfitting-for a matrix that come as close as possible to those of a target matrix (Schönemann, 1966).

text.text: Thus, in addition to testing for configural invariance, targeted orthogonal Procrustes rotation tests whether the sizes of the loadings are similar across samples, a property known as 'metric invariance'.

A well-understood index of how well factor loadings, item loadings, and the entire structure replicate can be used to determine how successfully, after targeted orthogonal Procrustes rotation, the factor loadings in one sample resemble the target loadings.
This index is known as Tucker's congruence coefficient (Haven & ten Berge, 1977) or ϕ.

text.text: Values of ϕ from 0.85 to 0.94 indicate fair similarity; values greater than or equal to 0.95 indicate equality; all other values indicate no similarity (Lorenzo-Seva & ten Berge, 2006).

text.text: Reading the critique, it seems as if M.M. worked under the assumption that, when they assign labels to factors that are the same or similar to those used by personality psychologists who study humans, comparative psychologists are signaling that the human and nonhuman factors are the same.
That is not the case.
Instead, using labels such as "Extraversion" when discussing personality factors in related species is like talking about a "forelimb".

Just because the same word is used does not mean that the things being described are identical: via adaptive radiation, among mammals, forelimbs are sometimes arms, sometimes wings, and sometimes flippers.
Labels such as "Extraversion" are not perfect, of course, and future work may identify more suitable labels, but that is not really problematic.
After all, these labels are hypotheses.
